analysis.one_liner: Requires independent inspections, health screening, and financial transparency for privatized military housing, and bars officials from owning stakes in it.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three weeks left in the 118th Congress and sent to three committees, it received no hearing, no vote, and expired when the Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Most military family housing on bases is run by private landlords. This bill would tighten oversight of those landlords: independent unannounced inspections, extension of normal federal, state, and local housing protections to on-base homes, public disclosure of the landlords' finances, and contract termination for landlords who breach their agreements. It would also add a health registry and VA disability presumptions for troops and families made sick by unsafe housing, and would bar members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, senior Pentagon officials, and generals from owning stakes in these housing companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Military families living in privatized base housing, where problems like mold, vermin, and deferred maintenance have been widely documented, along with veterans and family members who develop illnesses linked to unsafe housing and would gain VA disability presumptions and VA health care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Military families in privatized base housing

how_it_helps.text: Requires regular building-code and health inspections of base housing by independent inspectors who are not employed by the landlord, and lets state and local inspectors inspect without notice to landlords [S2].
Extends all federal, state, and local housing protections, including habitability standards and defenses to eviction, to people living on military installations [S2].

Requires the Pentagon to rescind a housing contract if the landlord commits a material breach and does not cure it within 90 days, and bars that landlord from new contracts or expansions; landlords could not mark maintenance work complete until an independent inspector approves it in writing [S2].

Requires annual publication in the Federal Register of the financial details of each housing contract, and requires landlords to file 10-K-equivalent financial statements that the Pentagon must post on a public website [S2].

Creates a screening program and public registry for troops and family members with health conditions tied to unsafe housing, and creates a VA presumption of service connection for illnesses associated with living in privatized military housing, with VA hospital and nursing home care for affected family members [S2].

Bars members of Congress serving on the House or Senate Armed Services Committees, senior Pentagon executives, and general and flag officers from owning any interest in an entity that owns or manages privatized military housing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The private companies that own and manage most military base housing, through inspections they do not control, public disclosure of their contract finances, the risk of losing contracts for uncured breaches, and loss of the ability to self-certify completed maintenance. Senior officials and lawmakers on the Armed Services Committees also lose the ability to hold ownership stakes in the sector.

drawbacks.text: The VA presumption of service connection and family-member health care would add claims and program costs for veterans' benefits, and family member care is funded only to the extent appropriations allow [S2].

Requiring housing offices at every installation to consist only of military department employees, staffing an independent inspector corps, and standing up a health registry would be a significant new administrative and budget burden for the Pentagon [S2].

Allowing a 90-day cure period followed by contract rescission creates real risk of disruption for families living in units managed by a company that loses its contract; the bill addresses this by requiring a written contingency plan for managing the housing, but the transition itself would be a disruption [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a concrete group of people with serious documented problems: families living in unsafe housing and veterans whose illnesses were linked to it. The costs fall mainly on the landlords being regulated and on Pentagon administration, which is the normal cost of oversight. The main honest objection is scale: building an inspection force and a health registry, plus expanding VA presumptions, is expensive, and the bill leaves the underlying privatization system in place rather than replacing it.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the final three weeks of the 118th Congress and split across three committees, it never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the bill on December 10, 2024, with three weeks remaining in the 118th Congress [S1][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to three committees: Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, and Judiciary, meaning three separate chairs would each have to act on their portions of it [S4].
It attracted 2 cosponsors, including a Republican, but no committee took any further action on it [S3][S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no other action after the initial referral; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The privatized military housing companies come out ahead: no inspection regime, no public disclosure of contract finances, no contract-termination penalty, and no ownership ban took effect. Military families in unsafe housing gained nothing.

industries.industry: Privatized military housing companies (private landlords that own and manage base housing)
industries.note: These companies collect service members' housing allowances as rent for homes on base. The bill would subject them to unannounced independent inspections, public disclosure of their contract finances, loss of contracts for uncured breaches, and an end to self-certifying their own maintenance work. Its provisions apply only when a landlord fails to meet standards, so compliant companies would keep their business; the companies that profit from lax oversight would lose that advantage.

industries.industry: Senior defense officials and Armed Services Committee members with investments
industries.note: The bill bars lawmakers on the Armed Services Committees, senior Pentagon executives, and general and flag officers from owning any interest in an entity that owns or manages privatized military housing, closing a channel by which officials with authority over these contracts could hold stakes in the companies they oversee.
